Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

vignette:
Claudia is a 39-year-old city council member who lives with her husband in a quiet suburban neighborhood. She grew up in a home where her father's rage was a weather system she learned to read before she could read words. The clearest memory she carries is from when she was seven: her father, red-faced, had backed her mother into the corner of the kitchen, his hand raised, her mother's body folded small against the cabinets. Claudia remembers the sharp angle of her own neck as she watched from the doorway-craned forward, frozen, unable to run or look away. She remembers the smell of burnt toast and the pattern of the linoleum. But there are gaps: she cannot recall how the argument started, what her mother said, or how it ended. She only knows that she stood there, body locked in that same craned-forward position, and that sometimes now, when a memory surfaces unbidden, she feels her neck tighten and her shoulders lift as though she is still standing in that doorway.

As an adult, Claudia has built a life around control and visibility. Her work on the council requires her to attend public meetings, shake hands in crowded rooms, and listen to constituents air grievances. She has come to believe that safety is something that must be actively maintained, and she has narrowed the places where she feels truly safe to just three: her home, her office with the door locked, and the back corner booth of a café she has frequented for years. In any other setting, her attention is divided. She watches people closely-their hands, their posture, the direction of their gaze. At a recent town hall, a man in the front row crossed his arms and leaned forward, and Claudia felt her throat close. She could not follow the question he was asking. Her mind had gone to her mother's face in that kitchen corner, and to the way her father's hand had looked as it rose. The memory had pulled her out of the room. She excused herself to the restroom and stood with her palms flat on the sink, trying to slow her breathing. What frightened her most was that she had not chosen the memory-it had simply arrived, and with it came the bodily feeling of being seven years old again, small and watchful, her neck craned forward.

The connection between the memory and her sense of threat has become tighter over the past year. The more the memory intrudes, the more dangerous the world feels afterward. She finds herself scanning rooms more aggressively, noticing exits, reading anger into neutral expressions. And the more she scans, the more the memory seems to surface-as though her vigilance is calling it up. She has trouble falling asleep because she lies in the dark replaying the gaps, trying to fill them in, and then her body tenses as though the scene is about to resume. Her husband has noticed that she flinches when he walks into a room too quickly. She has stopped attending evening community events unless she can sit with her back to a wall. At a recent zoning board meeting, she caught herself staring at a councilman's hands as he gestured, and she lost the thread of the discussion entirely. She left early, claiming a headache, and spent the rest of the evening in her locked office, certain that something bad was about to happen.

What finally brought Claudia to seek help was a moment last month when she could not enter the council chamber at all. She stood in the hallway, watching through the glass, and felt the familiar craning in her neck. She turned around and went home. She is afraid that if she does not understand why her own mind keeps pulling her back to that kitchen, she will lose the career she has worked for-and worse, she will keep living inside that doorway.
